en: Let his horse run and flew his bird.
“The season is nearing spring,” he said,
“The lowland grass has grown full;
Along the shore of Ala-Köl,
All the geese and ducks
Have gathered as thickly as a beating swarm.
The caravaner has taken to the road;
The season of migrating birds has come,
And my needed journey has arrived.
The White Falcon upon my hand,
With twelve tail feathers and ten flight feathers,
Preens every one without exception
And keeps looking toward the sky.
He flutters and strains against the perch,
Rears back and flies in reverse.
The season of migrating birds has come;
He cries out and will not stay upon his perch.
Day and night he never stops,
Giving out his piercing voice,
It resounds over him with a clatter.
If I do not fly my bird at the swans today,
If I do not have him take a swan from the lake
And drink my fill of joy—
They say a swan's gall is precious,
They say that precious thing is medicine.
If I do not return after taking a swan,
If I do not see the delight
Of the falcon upon my hand,
If, in her old age, I do not give swan meat
To Kanykey,
And to aged Chyyrdy,
If I do not see the prowess
Of the falcon left to me as a gift
By my heroic father Manas...”
“Who poured blood into black water,
Born beyond counting from
The gray wolf, the male leopard—Semetey,
My morning star beneath the crescent brow,
Lord in the midst
Of the Argyn and the Kyrgyz.
This ruinous gray wolf of a son
Grew eager for the falcon.
“Let him wear these when flying the falcon,”
Said my extraordinary mother Kanykey,
“And let him know my esteem.”
She lined the inside with silk,
Had it sewn with close stitches,
Folded it like a snake's belly,
And had silk wound around its cuff.
“Let him wear it with a wide sleeve,” she said.
Kanykey made the white glove,
A glove fitted to young Semetey;
He took it and put it on his hand.
The falcon upon the perch
He promptly took upon his hand.
His personal retinue numbered twenty-five,
All of them sons of khans:
Külchoro, son of Almambet,
Was a blessed guide when sent ahead;
Kanchoro, son of Khan Chubak,
Was like a countless host when leading them.
Kalyk, son of Sarykhan—
If an enemy came out to grapple,
His light brought advantage.
Baytaylak, son of Khan Bakay,
Had not yet ridden into battle,
And did not yet know an enemy's worth.
Oh, his form in this world!
Oh, this fine son of his father!
Shayymbet, son of Jamgyrchy,
Was another spirited young man.
Külchoro, son of Almambet,
Hurriedly saddled
The weary Buurul,
Hurriedly saddled the horse,
In the time it takes to open and close the eyes,
He saddled faster than the swiftest.
The white saddle made by Almambet
Had a front bow of white gold,
A rear bow of solid silver,
And two sides of broad iron;
He set the matchless saddle
Upon Buurul and stood ready,
He rode straight toward the encampment,
Readying the falcon for Semetey.
At twelve years old Külchoro
Was a blazing red ember;
The worth of all the others together
Could not produce a youth like him.
Girding on a silver belt,
The smiling orphan's
Sunlike face was touched by light.
Looking to either side,
Licking his lips,
He saw fourteen horses descended from Ogoy:
The mighty swift horse Buurul,
Kanykey's Karakaska courser,
Chyyrdy's Bozjorgo,
Chachykey's Tiktoru,
The inheritance left by his father,
The true swift horse Taytoru,
Sarykhan's Tuuchunak,
Khan Bakay's Kökcholok,
Abyke's Aktelki,
Khan Köbösh's Köktelki,
And the bay stallion Archatoru
Prepared by that hero,
Shayymbet's Akkökül,
And the girl's Kyzyljorgo.
Upon the heads of the fourteen horses
Were white halters knotted in rounded fashion;
With mighty Bakay at their head,
They had made fitted halters of that kind.
Growing eager, he had them matched together;
With coverings impervious to arrows,
He had all fourteen horses covered.
For a journey of extended lodging,
That orphan of Manas
Had tents and provisions
Loaded upon Nartelki.
He had abundant provisions packed,
As though departing for months and years—
That mad son of Manas
Had abundant provisions packed,
Prayed to his God,
And put on his weapons of war.
From there toward Ala-Köl,
He intended to roam throughout it:
“I shall fly my bird at the swans;
I shall have it take a swan.
Even if it is only a swan,
I myself shall drink my fill of joy.”
Semetey rode out in excitement;
The pampered wife Chachykey
Would not release him and cried aloud.
Wrapping herself around his stirrup leather,
Entangling herself in his reins,
Behaving more and more affectionately,
She tormented the hero
And led him back toward the encampment:
“Month after month, saying you will fly the falcon,
You go wandering away
And cast me into misery.
Saying, ‘I shall fly the falcon every day,’
You remain there boasting;
Going out upon the steppe each day,
You leave me longing for you.
Seven days are the measure of the sun;
For those seven days, my lord,
Do not fly your bird at swans,
And do not drink your fill of delight.
Do not rise and go toward the horses
And leave me in such great pain!”
Blood rushed into his dark face,
And the true son of the tiger
Now recovered his fury:
“Let go of my arm, woman;
Do not stand across my path.
While you lay there ill,
It seems you never truly recovered;
You have grown full of dreams and fancies,
And have become impossible.
Does a man not know his falcon,
And a woman not know her work?
Does she not know the head of the man,
Nor the order proper to a brave,
Nor even know herself as a woman?
I let you live freely as you pleased,
And pampered and cherished you so much
That you grew spoiled beyond measure,
And became witless, it appears!
You cooled and weakened my words,
And brought disgrace upon me;
Knowing so many muddled speeches,
You have turned out well indeed.
I went about thinking you were ill,
But you have turned out to be a bakshy!”
Semetey’s heavy whip,
Whose stroke could deafen the ear,
Made the defiant woman
Stagger beneath its blow.
Yesterday he had cured an ox hide,
Stretched it over a wooden core,
Cut the hide of a barren mare
Into narrow winding strips,
And bound it tightly around it.
He had an elm from Opol-Too’s foot
Torn out together with its root
And turned into the whip’s handle;
He had its waist wrapped in hide,
And had Bölekbay fit the shaft.
Its palm-piece was set with glass,
Its wrist-loop was of bargektüü leather;
Semetey seized the black-jawed whip,
Gripped it and bent it back,
Made the woman cry “Kank!”
And lashed her across the ribs.
May God spare one from such a sight:
Her billowing mottled dress
Split apart at the waist,
And her blood poured out in streams;
Her cherished patterned dress
Split open along the side,
And her blood flowed in waves.
Poor Chachykey the woman,
Like a mountain grouse upon a ridge,
Collapsed and crawled away;
From beneath her blue patterned silk dress
Her blood streamed down its hem.
The flesh of her side was torn,
And your poor, delicate sister-in-law
Fled inside screaming.
Her forefather was Tügöl Khan,
Blessed from his roots by Kydyr;
He had brought the woman to submission.
As for the blue-maned champion
Born after his father, the hero Manas,
He wore out horses and ranged the land,
Loosed his hounds and flew his birds,
And wandered about in revelry.
The delicate woman Chachykey,
From her softly gleaming eyes,
Shed tears in separate streams;
She screamed and wept and cried aloud,
Truly wept and sobbed,
And cried out in anguish.
She called Kulchoro and Kanchoro,
Summoning both of them together;
What your poor, delicate sister-in-law
Said to them was this—
When the two boys came to her,
Then she spoke these words:
“Turn your horse’s head around;
Boys, halt at the place ahead.
I have seen a dream,
And have many duties to entrust to you.
Know that I speak with sorrow;
My dear boys, heed my words!
Your prancing prince is no baseborn man;
Do not let your swaggering lord
Set his bird upon the swan,
Or seize the white swan where it rests!
He is riding away in fierce anger;
May he go safely and return sound.
Let my eyes see my prince
Together with his noble falcon;
Bring them safely back to me.
If either one of the two is lost,
Boys, may my eyes never see again!
Do not let him cross by the broad ford,
Or let a caravan carry news of him.
Go in health and return alert;
Come swiftly, before I begin to yearn.
Go in peace and return sound;
Come soon, before I grow weary.
If you commit some wicked deed, it will be shameful;
